Letter from the editor: Get comfortable with changing your mind

Happy FDOC, Deacs!
Mattie Stillerman, Editor-in-Chief
August 24, 2026
Categories:
  • Opinion
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:17
Instaread

This letter represents the view of Old Gold & Black Editor-in-Chief Mattie Stillerman, not the Old Gold & Black.

I blinked, and now I am a senior. 

Suddenly the way-too-short bob I had as a freshman has grown into long hair I can’t keep out of my face. My twin bed in Collins has turned into a queen in a house on Polo Road. The brand-new Wake Forest sweatshirt I was gifted at my high school graduation is extremely worn. Instead of my little brother moving me into college, I lugged his stuff into his freshman dorm. 

I blinked, and now the clueless staff writer is serving her last semester as editor-in-chief. 

Story continues below advertisement

– – – – – – – – – – – – – – – – – – – – – – 

As the oldest daughter and oldest granddaughter, I love giving unsolicited advice to my younger brother and younger cousins. This fall, four of us grandchildren will be in college, with my brother and two cousins moving into their freshman dorms. As I have now aged into an old and decrepit senior, I thought of what advice I should give them—what advice I would have wanted to hear as a new first-year at Wake Forest.

So here it goes.

There is going to be a lot of change in your life going forward. As soon as you get settled into one thing, you will be faced with new challenges and shifts. I don’t say this to scare you. In fact, I say it to excite you. 

Young adulthood is more complex than your childhood years. It comes with more independence, more opportunities and broader networks. Relationships become more intricate, your worldview becomes less black and white and you start to discover who you are outside of your hometown bubble. 

Yes, you will have to make difficult decisions and you will need to decide how you handle obstacles. All of this is worth the growth you will experience to become the person you will be.

I don’t have much more life figured out than I did when I was 18, but I have been exposed to possibilities I could never have imagined. Before college, I had never been outside of the country. Now, I have lived in South Africa and Spain, and have visited over 10 countries. I started as a pre-medical student, dead set on matriculating straight into medical school. After working for non-profits and writing for the Old Gold & Black, I have decided to go to law school (a decision I made my junior spring). 

So dear freshman (or sophomore or junior), it is perfectly all right to change your mind. You should change it at least a couple dozen times as you are exposed to new people, new experiences and new ways of thinking. You did not come to college because you already know it all. College is not just an experience to confirm what you already know—it is meant to challenge what you think you already know. 

Be open to new opportunities and ideas. Critically engage your new environment and make the most of your time as a Demon Deacon. As you grow into young adulthood, start to get comfortable with changing your mind.

Happy FDOC!

Mattie Stillerman, Editor-in-Chief

Mattie Stillerman is a junior from Charlotte, N.C., majoring in health and exercise science with minors in Spanish and biology. She is a member of Alpha Delta Pi, Jam for Janey and Alpha Epsilon Delta. Outside of the newsroom, Mattie enjoys cheering on the Demon Deacons, walking in Reynolda Village and grabbing matcha with friends.
